data.title: Mercedes-AMG GT SUV Deep Dive: Why heat matters more than horsepower in this electric monster
data.description:
The Mercedes-AMG GT SUV can produce a staggering 860kW. But the more interesting question is what happens after the first few seconds of full-throttle acceleration.

Delivering enormous power in an electric vehicle is one challenge. Delivering it repeatedly, without the motors, battery and electronics overheating and forcing a reduction in output, is quite another.

That’s the engineering problem AMG is tackling with its new electric performance flagship. Alongside its 860kW peak output, the GT 63 SUV is rated at 530kW continuously, with an arsenal of compact axial-flux motors, individually cooled battery cells and sophisticated thermal management designed to keep the performance coming.

READ MORE: Best luxury EVs in Australia 2026: Premium electric cars under $100k, $150k, $250k and beyond, priced and compared

READ MORE: Unveiled: The new Mercedes-AMG GT 4-Door EV has so much tech it makes the Porsche Taycan look very yesterday
READ MORE: Is this the sensible supercar? Mercedes-AMG GT 53 EV revealed with less power but 112km more range than crazy axial-flux 860kW flagship
READ MORE: 2026 Porsche Cayenne Turbo EV Brief Drive: This vehicle is brilliant, but all sorts of wrong

The technology is significant beyond the headline numbers, although how effectively it works remains to be established in independent testing.

Mercedes-Benz Australia lists the GT SUV as coming soon, with local pricing and specifications still to be confirmed.

The GT SUV range comprises three all-wheel drive models. The entry-level GT 53 produces 400kW and 800Nm from two conventional electric motors, while the GT 55 steps up to three axial-flux motors producing 600kW and 1860Nm.

The flagship GT 63 uses the same three-motor configuration but increases peak output to 860kW and 2000Nm.

The GT 55 and GT 63 share a claimed continuous output of 530kW, despite their substantially different peak ratings.

All three models use 800-volt electrical architecture, with battery capacities of 106kWh or 128kWh depending on the variant.

Where the heat comes from

An EV converts stored electrical energy into motion through its battery, inverters and motors. Each stage incurs losses, some of which become heat that must be removed.

A short acceleration run can use some of the system’s capacity to absorb heat. Repeated acceleration or sustained high speed requires heat to be carried away quickly enough to prevent temperatures continually rising.

Cooling from inside the battery outwards

The battery’s ability to deliver power depends partly on the temperature of individual cells. An acceptable average pack temperature can conceal a local hot spot that forces the control system to reduce output.

Many liquid-cooled EV batteries transfer heat through a plate or other cooling structure adjoining the cells. AMG instead circulates electrically non-conductive oil directly around each cylindrical cell.

Both approaches must conduct heat out of the cell’s interior. Direct cooling brings the fluid to the cell casing, reducing the intervening structures through which that heat must pass.

AMG also uses narrow cells, measuring 26mm across and 105mm tall. Their diameter limits the distance between the core and the cooled outer surface. An aluminium casing helps conduct heat, while a full-tab design reduces internal electrical resistance, according to the company.

Moving heat is only the first step

Oil passing around the cells carries heat away from them, but the vehicle still has to dispose of that heat. Cooling capacity is also needed by the motors and their power electronics.

AMG’s Central Coolant Hub coordinates pumps, valves and sensors to allocate cooling according to demand. Its wider thermal system includes a chiller and main and auxiliary radiators.

If the battery is already at the required temperature, the system can direct cooling capacity towards the drive units. When several components are working hard, it must balance their competing needs.

Why the motors are shaped differently

The GT 55 and GT 63 use axial-flux motors developed from technology supplied by Mercedes-owned British specialist YASA.

Their disc-shaped layout places a stator between two magnet-equipped rotors, with magnetic flux running parallel to the shaft. The arrangement offers high torque and power density in a short package.

YASA identifies short copper windings and direct oil cooling as advantages for sustained output, helping remove heat before temperature becomes a constraint.

The rear drive unit combines two motors and their gearboxes, with oil cooling for the motors and gears. Water-cooled silicon-carbide inverters convert the battery’s direct current into the supply the motors require.

Separate rear motors allow driving force to be varied at each rear wheel, changing the turning effect on the vehicle and helping control its path.

Saving capacity for the useful parts of a lap

AMG’s Predictive Performance Manager adjusts power according to the track section, conserving electrical and thermal capacity where extra output offers little lap-time benefit.

A tight downhill sequence, for example, offers less opportunity to exploit full power than an uphill straight. Reducing demand in the former can leave more capacity available for the latter.

Controlling the body without conventional anti-roll bars

The GT 63’s Active Ride Control+ suspension uses a central pump, controlled valves and hydraulically interconnected dampers to generate forces opposing body movement. It replaces conventional anti-roll bars and is optional on the GT 55.

A mechanical anti-roll bar links suspension movement across an axle. It resists roll, but can also transmit a disturbance from one side towards the other. Hydraulic control allows AMG to vary the support according to the driving situation, including pitch under acceleration and braking.

Adjustable air springs control ride characteristics and height. The aim is support during manoeuvres with compliance over uneven roads.

The system still has to manage the SUV’s mass. Its effectiveness requires assessment of grip, ride quality and consistency, alongside how flat the body remains.

There is no confirmed timetable for this combination of motors, battery cooling and active suspension to reach affordable EVs. The demonstrated expansion is within AMG itself, from the electric GT 4-Door Coupe to the GT SUV.

data.title: Latest ANCAP results: BYD Sealion 8 puts BYD back on five-star footing after Sealion 5 setback
data.description:
BYD has bounced back from a three-star ANCAP setback with a five-star rating for the new Sealion 8.

ANCAP marked down the seven-seat plug-in hybrid SUV after the driver’s footwell split in a frontal crash test, but it retained the maximum rating.

But back in September the the smaller BYD Sealion 5 SUV, managed only three stars. Both SUVs were assessed under ANCAP’s latest 2026-2028 protocols.

READ MORE: Best EVs to buy in Australia 2026: The ultimate guide to affordable electric cars at every price

READ MORE: Three-star setback: BYD Sealion 5 breaks brand’s perfect ANCAP run as M9 people-mover scores five
READ MORE: GAC Aion UT and XPeng X9 earn five ANCAP stars under tougher 2026 safety tests, but where are the knobs?
READ MORE: Cheap EVs clear tougher new ANCAP safety tests: Geely EX2 and Leapmotor B05 score five stars

The split opened behind the brake and accelerator pedals. ANCAP said it did not increase the injury risk measured by the driver dummy, but warned such a failure can raise the risk of lower-leg injuries.

The Sealion 8 scored 90 per cent for crash protection, 76 per cent for crash avoidance, 73 per cent for safe driving and 100 per cent for post-crash safety. The rating covers all Australian and New Zealand variants.

The Sealion 5 remains the only model assessed under the new protocols to fall short of five stars, according to ANCAP. Its weakest scores were 48 per cent for safe driving and 51 per cent for crash avoidance.

The Sealion 8 also earned full marks for the layout and operation of its essential controls. That was an area where the five-star GAC Aion UT and XPeng X9 lost points in October over their reliance on touchscreens.

The electric GWM Ora 5 also earned five stars, covering both Lux and Ultra variants. It scored 91 per cent for crash protection and 92 per cent for post-crash safety.

ANCAP said its automatic emergency braking and lane-keeping systems generally performed well, although avoiding cars, motorcycles and pedestrians at lower speeds proved more challenging.

The Sealion 8 was tested by ANCAP, while the Ora 5 was tested by EuroNCAP and the results verified by the local safety authority.

data.title: Jetour TX electric SUV launches: Chery-owned SUV brand is coming to Australia and this is its first EV
data.description:
Jetour has opened Chinese pre-sales for its new TX electric SUV, adding a potential battery-powered contender to its Australian expansion plans as the Chery-owned brand prepares for its local debut.

Combining boxy styling, rear- and all-wheel drive options and a claimed driving range of up to 550km, the TX brings a dedicated electric platform to a brand whose initial Australian range is expected to centre on the T1 and T2 PHEV SUVs.

With the local launch only days away, Jetour Australia says there is no announcement on a local introduction for the TX.

READ MORE: Best EVs to buy in Australia 2026: The ultimate guide to affordable electric cars at every price

READ MORE: New 575kW Jetour Traveller 7 revealed: Rugged PHEV packs 245km EV range as Chinese brand prepares for Australia

“The TX shows the depth of Jetour’s global line-up, including its first fully electric SUV,” a Jetour Australia spokesperson told EV Central.

“We’re always looking at which models best suit Australian drivers, but we have nothing to announce on the TX at this stage.

“Jetour is coming to Australia with a line-up of adventure-ready SUVs built for the way Australians travel and explore, and we’ll share more about our Australian models very soon.”

Chinese pre-sales opened on November 16, with five variants priced from 99,900 to 145,900 yuan ($22.400 to $37,400 approx). Those are domestic pre-sale prices and provide no indication of what an Australian version might cost.

The TX’s upright body, circular lighting and contrasting exterior trim continue Jetour’s preference for rugged-looking SUVs, although this model is built on a purpose-designed rear-wheel drive electric platform.

It measures 1880mm wide and 1700mm tall, with a 2735mm wheelbase. Overall length is quoted at 4605mm including its tailgate-mounted storage box, or 4475mm without it – putting the body close to the size of a BYD Atto 3.

Rear-wheel drive versions produce 200kW and 285Nm, with a claimed 0-100km/h time of 7.5 seconds. The dual-motor all-wheel drive flagship lifts combined outputs to 275kW and 427Nm and cuts that sprint to 5.5 seconds.

The Chinese range comprises four rear-drive variants claiming 550km of range and an all-wheel drive version rated at 510km. Both figures use China’s relatively generous CLTC test cycle.

Practical features include a 150-litre front storage compartment, while the cabin has a 15.6-inch central touchscreen and an 8.8-inch digital instrument display. Higher grades offer additional parking and driving assistance functions for the Chinese market.

The TX also supports vehicle-to-load output of up to 6.6kW, allowing its battery to supply external electrical equipment.

Its emergence comes ahead of Jetour’s expected late-November Australian brand launch, with the T1 and T2 already holding local vehicle approvals ahead of anticipated showroom arrivals in early 2027. Approval does not confirm every listed powertrain will be offered at launch.

Jetour has also flagged a naming change: a November 18 announcement says the T2 is expected to carry the Jetour 20 badge in Australia. Its local plug-in hybrid specification and inclusion in the initial range remain unannounced. Jetourt has also issued photography of the Jetour 20 in disguise in Sydney.

Australian ROVER filings list the T1 with petrol and plug-in hybrid powertrains. The petrol version pairs a 180kW 2.0-litre turbocharged four-cylinder with a seven-speed dual-clutch transmission. The PHEVs combine a 105kW 1.5-litre turbo-petrol engine with a 150kW front electric motor, while the all-wheel drive version adds a 175kW rear motor. The filing lists “maximum possible” drivetrain outputs of 255kW and 430kW respectively, rather than confirmed combined system ratings.

The T2/20 is listed with an all-wheel drive plug-in hybrid powertrain combining a 105kW 1.5-litre turbocharged four-cylinder petrol engine with three electric motors: 90kW and 75kW units at the front and a 175kW rear motor. The filing lists maximum possible drivetrain power of 445kW, although that should not be treated as a confirmed combined system output. Australian battery capacity and electric driving range remain unannounced.

data.title: Mitsubishi ASX VR-e range and servicing confirmed: Here’s how far it will go and how much it costs to maintain
data.description:
Mitsubishi has officially confirmed its new ASX VR-e compact electric SUV will travel up to 403km on a charge under WLTP testing, although the dual-motor flagship GSR gives up 75km of claimed range for its second motor and all-wheel drive.

Mitsubishi has also confirmed capped-price servicing costs for the electric SUV, starting at $199 for the first scheduled visit.

All four versions use the same 57.7kWh lithium iron phosphate battery supplied by CATL. The rear-drive LS has the longest range at 403km, followed by the Aspire at 398km and the Exceed at 380km. The 342kW GSR is rated at 328km.

READ MORE: Best EVs to buy in Australia 2026: The ultimate guide to affordable electric cars at every price

READ MORE:
READ MORE: A different Pajero PHEV? Mitsubishi wants smaller plug-in hybrid SUV for Australia
READ MORE: Mitsubishi bets buyers will pay more for ASX VR-e: Dealer network and warranty underpin challenge to cheaper Chinese EVs

For comparison, Kia claims 436km for the EV3 Air Standard Range, 33km more than the Mitsubishi LS.

Mitsubishi claims a 10-80 per cent DC charge takes about 30 minutes, with charging power peaking at 134kW. AC charging tops out at 6.6kW, with a 10-100 per cent charge taking about 10 hours at that rate.

A portable Mode 2 cable is standard, and a Mode 3 cable is available as a dealer accessory. All four grades can also power compatible external equipment through the charging port using vehicle-to-load.

The ASX VR-e is due for servicing every 12 months or 15,000km, whichever comes first. Under Mitsubishi’s capped-price schedule, the first five services total $1495 and the first 10 total $4490.

The sixth, eighth and tenth services are the most expensive at $799 each. The schedule covers the first 10 years or 150,000km, whichever comes first, with work outside the scheduled services costing extra.

Mitsubishi’s vehicle warranty runs for up to 10 years or 200,000km if all scheduled servicing is completed on time at a Mitsubishi dealer. Otherwise, the vehicle warranty is five years or 100,000km.

The separate battery warranty runs for eight years or 160,000km, with a capacity guarantee of at least 70 per cent of usable energy over that period.

The ASX VR-e also gets a dedicated phone app that lets owners check charge status and estimated completion time, view charging history and remotely control the climate system, locks and windows. Mitsubishi says the car can receive software updates over the air.

data.title: Mitsubishi ASX VR-e priced: Electric SUV undercuts arch-rival Kia EV3 but the Chinese are cheaper
data.description:
Mitsubishi will launch its first battery-electric model in Australia since the i-MiEV at $45,990 drive-away, with the four-model ASX VR-e range topping out at $68,990 drive-away for the dual-motor GSR.

The entry-level LS has a recommended retail price of $46,740 before on-road costs, but Mitsubishi’s national launch offer puts it on the road for $750 less than its list price. The Aspire is $53,990 on either basis. Mitsubishi says the ASX VR-e will reach showrooms in late 2026.

2027 Mitsubishi ASX VR-e pricing and range

LS RWD: $46,740 plus on-road costs / $45,990 launch drive-away / 403km WLTP
Aspire RWD: $53,990 plus on-road costs / $53,990 launch drive-away / 398km WLTP
Exceed RWD: $57,990 plus on-road costs / $58,990 launch drive-away / 380km WLTP
GSR AWD: $64,990 plus on-road costs / $68,990 launch drive-away / 328km WLTP

READ MORE: Best EVs to buy in Australia 2026: The ultimate guide to affordable electric cars at every price

READ MORE: Mitsubishi bets buyers will pay more for ASX VR-e: Dealer network and warranty underpin challenge to cheaper Chinese EVs
READ MORE: The 2027 Mitsubishi ASX VR-e explained: How Taiwanese phone maker Foxconn helped Mitsubishi return to the Australian EV race
READ MORE: Fastest Mitsubishi yet: 342kW ASX VR-e electric SUV confirmed for Australia, with starting price expected in the $40,000s

The LS undercuts the Kia EV3 Air Standard Range by $860 on list price. Mitsubishi has identified the smallest Kia EV as this car’s key rival.

The Kia lists at $47,600 before on-road costs but there is a $46,990 drive-away offer current, $1000 above Mitsubishi’s national launch offer.

But Chinese rivals are cheaper. For example, the larger Geely EX5 starts at $41,990 before on-road costs, making it $4750 cheaper than the Mitsubishi on list price.

The gap is even bigger at the budget end. GWM’s Ora 5 Lux is advertised from $33,990 drive-away for private buyers in Victoria, $12,000 below the ASX LS even before GWM’s additional November discount on eligible stock.

Mitsubishi previously told EV Central it believed its dealer network and warranty would give buyers a reason to pay more than they would for cheaper Chinese EVs.

The Taiwan-built ASX VR-e is based on the Foxtron Bria and uses a dedicated EV platform. It shares its name with Mitsubishi’s petrol ASX, which is based on the Renault Captur. The LS, Aspire and Exceed all use a 171kW rear motor, while the GSR adds a front motor for all-wheel drive and a combined 342kW.

Mitsubishi ASX VR-e model walk

LS: The base model has 18-inch alloys, cloth upholstery, manually adjustable front seats, dual-zone climate control, a reversing camera and rear parking sensors.

It also gets a 15.6-inch touchscreen, a 9.2-inch driver display, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, a portable charging cable and vehicle-to-load capability.

Aspire: For another $8000 at launch, the Aspire adds synthetic leather, heated and ventilated power front seats, driver’s seat memory and ambient lighting.

It also gets a front boot with an electric bonnet release, an adjustable rear cargo floor, adaptive high beams, front parking sensors, a 360-degree camera and parking assistance.

Exceed: Another $5000 adds 20-inch two-tone alloys, a panoramic glass roof, a hands-free powered tailgate and a 12-speaker SEAS audio system. Claimed range falls from the Aspire’s 398km to 380km.

GSR: A further $10,000 buys the dual-motor all-wheel-drive system, along with microsuede seat inserts, blue stitching and black-roof paint options.

Mitsubishi claims a 3.9-second 0-100km/h time using a rollout method. The GSR also has the shortest claimed range of the four grades at 328km.

data.title: Polestar 4 OTA update: Electric SUV family gains 3.3kW vehicle-to-load and camping mode in software update
data.description:
Polestar is rolling out an over-the-air update that allows the Polestar 4 to power appliances and tools from its battery, adding a function that existing owners can use with a separately sold adaptor.

The P4.3.0 update also brings a camping mode and upgrades the car’s infotainment system to Android Automotive OS 15.

While some countries will miss out on some features, Polestar Australia says they are all coming here.

READ MORE: Best EVs to buy in Australia 2026: The ultimate guide to affordable electric cars at every price

READ MORE: Polestar 4 Coupe price slashed: Up to $4600 discounts bring it inline with new Polestar 4 SUV
READ MORE: Polestar 4 SUV revealed and priced: More practical EV gets rear window, 630km range and undercuts coupe on dollars
READ MORE: Another Polestar 4 update rolls in: Top-selling Swede has better handling, is more sustainable and Dual Motor cops a price cut!

Vehicle-to-load (V2L) can supply up to 3.3kW through an adaptor plugged into the car’s charging port. That’s fine for camping.

Owners can use it to run equipment such as a camping fridge or power tools, and set a minimum battery charge level at which the car stops supplying power.

Camping mode maintains the selected cabin temperature and keeps V2L, USB and 12-volt outlets active while the car is parked. It switches off automatically when the battery reaches 20 per cent. A separate valet mode restricts access to vehicle settings and lets the owner set a maximum speed and lock the glovebox.

The update extends digital key support to compatible Google and Samsung phones, following the introduction of Apple support in 2025. It lets drivers lock, unlock and start the car with their phone. Polestar will send activation codes to primary drivers as it enables the feature in each market.

Park Assist Pilot is limited to MY26 and MY27 cars fitted with the Pilot Pack. Once the driver selects a perpendicular parking space and confirms the manoeuvre, the system takes over steering and braking. Polestar says hardware differences rule out the feature for MY25 cars.

The release also revises how Google Maps estimates energy use, taking into account live consumption and accessories such as trailers and load carriers.

Polestar says the update improves the response of remote controls in its phone app and the speed at which the car’s displays start up.

Owners will see a notification on the centre display when the download is available.

The software rollout coincides with the expansion of the Australian Polestar 4 range. The new SUV body style adds a conventional rear window and more luggage space alongside the original Coupe, which uses a camera in place of a rear window.

September’s price cuts brought the Coupe into line with the SUV, with both starting at $73,900 before on-road costs in Rear Motor guise and $81,750 for the Dual Motor.

data.title: EV owners dodging peak power prices: 80 per cent of grid charging happens off-peak
data.description:
New data sourced from an EV home charger supplier shows its customers are drawing around 80 per cent of their grid-sourced charging electricity during cheaper off-peak periods.

The finding supplied by the smart-charger manufacturer Evnex offers a snapshot of how customers across its Australian and New Zealand network manage home charging costs, with rooftop solar counted separately.

Evnex says its dataset comprises approximately 23,000 connected chargers – 13,000 in Australia and 10,000 in New Zealand.

READ MORE: Best EVs to buy in Australia 2026: The ultimate guide to affordable electric cars at every price

READ MORE: You can save how much? As fuel prices rise a new survey reveals the growing cost advantage of EVs
READ MORE: Shock findings: Switching to an EV electricity plan could save drivers up to $1800 a year, but not every deal stacks up
READ MORE: Home EV charging explained: Everything you need to know

The records extend back to approximately 2018, although the company says most charging data was collected over the past 12 months as its network expanded.

The 80 per cent figure measures the share of grid-sourced electricity consumed off-peak. It does not mean 80 per cent of owners charge exclusively at cheaper times, and the results should not be treated as representative of all Australian EV drivers.

Nevertheless, the figures highlight a straightforward opportunity to reduce running costs: change when the car charges.

“A typical EV uses around 2,000 kilowatt-hours a year. Pay 30 cents [per kWh] for that electricity and it costs you $600. Pay 15 cents and it’s $300. Same car, same driving, half the bill,” said Evnex founder and CEO Ed Harvey.

That example represents an annual saving of $300 without reducing the distance driven.

Evnex separately estimates savings of around $320 annually for a household shifting from predominantly peak charging to a smart charging schedule, rising to around $600 in higher-cost peak charging scenarios.

Those figures are modelled estimates rather than savings measured across its charger network. The company has not supplied the specific electricity plans or charging schedules behind them, and actual savings will depend on consumption, tariffs and how much charging can be moved.

Harvey says EVs offer households greater flexibility than many other electricity-consuming appliances.

“Most households can’t move their cooking or evening heating into a cheap power window. An EV is different. It sits in the driveway for hours, it doesn’t care when it charges, and a smart charger moves that charging to the cheapest window automatically,” he said.

For eligible households, the cheapest charging opportunity can now include free daytime grid electricity.

The Federal Government’s Solar Sharer Offer became available on July 1, 2026, in NSW, South Australia and south-east Queensland. It provides eligible households with smart meters access to three hours of free daytime electricity, capped at the first 24kWh per day across the household. Rooftop solar is not required.

However, choosing a plan requires more than comparing its cheapest charging window. Daily supply charges and electricity prices outside the free period still matter, particularly for households using substantial power in the evening.

The Australian Government’s Energy Made Easy service warns that higher rates outside the free window can affect whether switching delivers an overall saving.

Owners with rooftop solar have another option: directing surplus generation into their car.

Using surplus solar can reduce electricity purchases, although owners should also consider any feed-in revenue they forgo and the cost of charging equipment.

Evnex sells chargers that schedule charging around electricity prices and, depending on the model and equipment fitted, divert surplus solar into the vehicle. Its Australian website advertises hardware from $799 and fully installed charging packages from $1700.

data.title: Tank attack! GWM confirms 2027 SUV expansion with 1195Nm PHEV and V8 flagships in the frame
data.description:
GWM will expand its Australian Tank SUV range in 2027, with the Denza B5-rivalling Tank 400 plug-in hybrid and the larger Tank 700 and 800 luxury off-roaders among the contenders.

The Tank 400 (pictured top), 700 and flagship 800 are all in the mix as the Chinese giant prepares to broaden a local range currently comprising the mid-size 300 and seven-seat 500.

GWM has also reaffirmed plans to introduce V8 power before the end of next year, while hybrid and plug-in hybrid diesel engines could also be seen in Australia as early as next year.

READ MORE: Best EVs to buy in Australia 2026: The ultimate guide to affordable electric cars at every price

READ MORE: GWM Tank 400 Hi4-Z PHEV brief drive: Torque monster Denza B5 rival likely for Australia
READ MORE: Massive 4500kg braked towing from a PHEV for under $100k? Tank 700 SUV could deliver that to Australia as soon as 2026
READ MORE: GWM’s EV and PHEV push: Ora Touring and bigger Jolion spearhead 16-product Australian expansion

“There’s a Tank 400. There’s a Tank 700. There’s a Tank 800. All those cars are available to us,” GWM Australia marketing and communications chief Steve Maciver said at the recent Haval H7 media launch.

“We’re doing the work right now to consider what we’ll take but there will be an expansion of the Tank range within next year.”

For plug-in hybrid buyers, the five-seat Tank 400 offers a particularly interesting prospect.

EV Central sampled its Hi4-Z version in China, where GWM claims combined outputs of 635kW and 1195Nm from a 2.0-litre turbo-petrol engine and two electric motors.

A substantial 59kWh battery supplies a claimed 200km of electric driving on the WLTC cycle, while an 800V electrical system supports DC charging at up to 163kW. These are overseas specifications; an Australian powertrain has yet to be selected.

The 400 is also available with GWM’s more traditional Hi4-T plug-in hybrid system, providing another option for the Australian operation.

Above it, the Tank 700 would give GWM a larger luxury off-roader to challenge the Toyota LandCruiser and Nissan Patrol.

Already offered overseas with V6 plug-in hybrid power, the Tank 700 is also confirmed to get GWM’s new V8. GWM has displayed the V8 in a plug-in hybrid powertrain.

Chairman Jack Wei identified Australia and New Zealand among the markets that helped justify developing the engine. However, Australian outputs, electrification details and pricing remain unconfirmed.

EV Central has previously reported the prospect of a V8 PHEV Tank 700 with 4500kg braked towing capacity. That remains a potential application rather than an announced Australian specification.

The larger Tank 800 is another possible home for V8 power. Earlier this year, GWM Australia product planning manager Tim Leong indicated it was headed here in 2027 and would sit on its own platform above the 700.

Maciver’s latest comments leave the final Australian model selection open.

GWM is also developing diesel hybrid and diesel plug-in hybrid powertrains, although Australian timing and model applications remain undecided. They would make sense for Tank, but also GWM’s ute brand Cannon.

“It’s not too far away,” Maciver said. “I don’t want to commit to definitely being next year.

“Development is continuing, they’re speaking to this market about what our needs are. We’ve seen the performance numbers, we’ve seen the specs and the details on it, and it’s certainly a compelling proposition.”

The Tank expansion forms part of at least 14 GWM launches planned for 2027 as it targets a top-five Australian sales ranking.

The large SUV roll-out by GWM also includes the seven-seat Haval H10, while the six-seat Wey V9X is expected in 2027 following the premium brand’s Australian launch.

data.title: Less than three hours charging during 5900km of driving: BMW i3 claims rapid-charge road trip record
data.description:
BMW says its new i3 electric sedan has travelled almost 5900km across Europe with less than three hours of charging, demonstrating how faster charging and lower energy consumption could cut waiting times on long-distance EV trips.

The dual-motor i3 50 xDrive covered 5886.7km from Norway’s North Cape to Tarifa in southern Spain, recording a combined charging time of two hours, 45 minutes and 54 seconds.

Perhaps more significant than its headline 400kW maximum charging capability, BMW says the car averaged 275kW across its charging sessions, using exclusively publicly accessible chargers.

READ MORE: Best EVs to buy in Australia 2026: The ultimate guide to affordable electric cars at every price

READ MORE: How far can an electric car really go? Every EV ranked for road trips
READ MORE: Wagons roll! 2027 BMW i3 Touring teased as Neue Klasse expansion continues
READ MORE: The iconic BMW 3 Series goes electric! Meet the 2027 Neue Klasse BMW i3 xDrive 50

The manufacturer also reported average energy consumption of 12.5kWh/100km across the eight-country journey – below its quoted WLTP combined consumption range of 13.4-18.0kWh/100km.

However, this was a BMW-run efficiency challenge with carefully planned charging stops, rather than an independent comparison test or a typical family holiday.

The quoted time covers charging during the journey. It does not establish the total time spent stopped for meals, rest breaks, charger access or other delays.

BMW has not detailed the number of charging stops, individual charging sessions or the battery’s starting and finishing charge levels in its announcement.

The drive formed part of the Paneuropeana challenge, which measures the lowest accumulated charging time over a route with specified checkpoints.

Participants can choose their charging locations, making route planning and access to suitable high-powered infrastructure important to the result.

BMW says its run beat the previous charging-time record, set in 2017, by more than seven hours.

Actual driving occupied 74 hours and 41 minutes, with the route taking in motorways, country roads and towns.

According to BMW, a single engineer occupied the test car throughout the drive. An identical i3 and an iX3 50 xDrive accompanied it as support vehicles.

The company says all three vehicles had hardware and software identical to the standard production specification available to customers.

The new i3 is BMW’s electric 3 Series sedan, reviving a name previously used for its compact electric hatchback.

In 50 xDrive form, it combines front and rear electric motors producing 345kW and 645Nm with a 108.7kWh usable battery.

BMW claims 0-100km/h acceleration in 4.7 seconds and a maximum WLTP driving range of 912km, depending on specification.

Its sixth-generation electric drivetrain includes an 800-volt electrical architecture and cylindrical battery cells, with DC charging capability of up to 400kW.

BMW says a suitable fast charger can add up to 423km of WLTP driving range in 10 minutes.

Efficiency measures include a drag coefficient of 0.21, which BMW describes as its lowest yet, and low rolling resistance tyres. The challenge car ran on 19-inch aerodynamic wheels.

BMW also claims its latest electric motors reduce energy losses by 40 per cent compared with the previous generation, while the new cylindrical battery cells improve volumetric energy density by 20 per cent.

data.title: Ora expansion gathers pace! New hatch firms as bigger electric SUV heads for Australia
data.description:
GWM’s Ora revival will gather pace in 2027, with a larger electric SUV due early in the year and a new hatchback firming for Australian showrooms.

Additional body styles are also under consideration as GWM builds the electric brand beyond the single-model presence that constrained its early years in Australia.

The next confirmed arrival is the Ora 5 Plus medium SUV (pictured top), scheduled for the first quarter of 2027.

It follows earlier Australian plans referring to a larger Ora SUV as the Touring, which GWM had hoped to introduce before the end of 2026. The latest timing puts the bigger SUV alongside the incoming Haval Jolion Max in GWM’s early-2027 rollout.

A lower-riding Ora 5 hatch is also moving closer, providing a successor to the discontinued original Ora hatch.

“The Ora hatch is in our plans. Again we haven’t announced details on that yet but the Ora hatch is something we are absolutely looking at and you’ll probably see that if we do go ahead with it sooner rather than later,” GWM Australia marketing and communications chief Steve Maciver said.

“But that’s one that’s firming for us at the moment.”

The prospective newcomer is based on the newer Ora 5 platform, rather than being a return of the original Australian model.

GWM has previously floated the possibility of a sub-$30,000 drive-away starting price for the hatch, although final pricing and battery specifications remain unsettled.

Maciver confirmed the broader Ora 5 family offered further opportunities.

“On that same Ora 5 platform there are additional body styles available to us that we’re looking at that aren’t yet locked in,” he said.

Beyond that family, the newly revealed Ora 7 provides another model to watch, although GWM has not confirmed it for Australia.

Revealed in fastback and shooting brake forms, the Ora 7 is substantially larger than the Ora 5. Chinese specifications include a dual-motor version producing 310kW and claimed driving range of up to 630km on the generous CLTC test cycle.

Ora’s expansion could eventually involve more than battery-electric models, with hybrid options available to the Australian operation.

“Ora will still remain mainly electric,” Maciver said.

“We’re still working out what we do with that.”

Ora arrived in Australia in 2023 with a single electric hatchback, but initially struggled to gain traction, recording 1225 sales in 2024 before slipping to 763 in 2025. The arrival of the larger Ora 5 SUV in June 2026 has lifted its contribution substantially: the newcomer delivered 2156 sales in its first five months, including 520 in October, comfortably eclipsing the original hatch’s best full-year result.

GWM Australia managing director Andrew Gao also claimed the Ora 5 had reached third place in its segment within three months of launch, although he did not specify the sales period or category definition.

Ora’s expansion forms part of GWM’s broader Australian product offensive, alongside Haval SUVs, Tank off-roaders, Cannon utes and the emerging Wey premium range, spanning electric, hybrid, plug-in hybrid, petrol and diesel power.

Currently seventh on the year-to-date sales ladder, GWM is targeting a top-five finish in 2027 and a top-three position longer term.

A stronger contribution from Ora will be important to those ambitions.

With Haval also adding battery-electric vehicles, Maciver said Ora’s distinctive design would help define its place within GWM’s growing portfolio.

“I think what does differentiate Ora is its styling. We’ve got this retro-futuristic styling, something that’s a little bit different,” he said.

“Whether you love it or whether you don’t, what you can say about Ora’s styling is that it is different, it is unique, and it does stand out.

“And that allows us to carve out a space and a niche within that increasingly crowded EV segment.”
